title: The adhan's words
hook: Allah is greatest, I testify, come to prayer, come to success, then the same at the start

segments.voice: Yesterday, tayammum, and your line: the earth is clean. Where did you find a way still open? This week: last words, then getting ready, with conditions, wudu, its breakers, ghusl, tayammum. Today, the call all that readiness answers. Day one thousand seventy-eight.

Come to success. Of everything a voice could shout from a rooftop at dawn, that's an odd choice. Not come to duty. Not come, or else. Come to success, hayya ala al-falah, called out over the street at each prayer time, to anyone within earshot. A delivery driver hears it at a red light. A student hears it through a dorm window. A grandmother hears it from a phone app in the kitchen. The whole call is a handful of short phrases. Today, the words themselves, in order, and how the call is built.
screen: `COME TO SUCCESS, FROM A ROOFTOP.` → `A DRIVER, A STUDENT, A GRANDMOTHER.` → `THE WORDS, IN ORDER.`

segments.voice: Sunan Abu Dawud, number 499, records the words as a companion, Abdullah ibn Zayd, received them. Listen to the shape. It opens: Allahu akbar, Allah is greatest. Then the two testimonies, the ones this path spent last week on: ashhadu an la ilaha illallah, I testify there is no god but Allah; ashhadu anna Muhammadan rasulullah, I testify that Muhammad is the messenger of Allah. Then two invitations. Hayya ala as-salah, come to prayer. Hayya ala al-falah, come to success. And then it closes the way it began: Allahu akbar, and la ilaha illallah. Notice the ring. The call starts with God's greatness and the testimony, swings out to the listener with two invitations, and comes home to the same words. For the dawn call, Sunan Abu Dawud, number 500, adds a line after the invitations: as-salatu khayrun min an-nawm, prayer is better than sleep. And earlier, this path heard how Shia Muslims add their own lines to the call. The listener has a part, too. In Sahih Muslim, number 385, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, teaches that when you hear the call you repeat each phrase after the caller, but at come to prayer and come to success you answer la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah: there is no power and no strength except with God. You're invited to success, and you answer that you can't get there on your own strength. The Qur'an names the call too, in Pickthall's translation: "When the call is heard for the prayer of the day of congregation, haste unto remembrance of Allah."
screen: `IT OPENS: ALLAH IS GREATEST.` · `TWO TESTIMONIES, TWO INVITATIONS.` · `IT CLOSES THE WAY IT BEGAN.` · `THE LISTENER ANSWERS: NO POWER BUT WITH GOD.` · then, large: `HAYYA ALA AL-FALAH. COME TO SUCCESS.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn the words. Settle, and say them with me, quietly, or just listen. Allahu akbar. Ashhadu an la ilaha illallah. Ashhadu anna Muhammadan rasulullah. Hayya ala as-salah. Hayya ala al-falah. Allahu akbar. La ilaha illallah. Now go back to the invitations and stay there. Come to prayer. Come to success. If you pray, you can practice the answer: la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah. If you don't, notice what the call names as success, and let the words sit. The bell holds the time.
The adhan's words. Greatness, two testimonies, two invitations, and greatness and testimony again, a call shaped like a ring. Today's word.
Your line: come to success. Today, the next time you hear the adhan, or a reminder on your phone, notice what it calls success. Tomorrow, the iqamah. Day one thousand seventy-eight.

howItsDone: A muezzin calls the adhan when each prayer time begins, from the mosque or over a speaker, and the hadith teaches those who hear it to repeat the phrases after him, answering the two invitations with la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah.

trapdoor: what you thought: the adhan is a long chant in Arabic.
what it means: a short set of phrases: greatness, two testimonies, come to prayer, come to success, and back again.
what a scholar hears: the words as recorded in Abu Dawud 499, the dawn line in 500, and the listener's answer in Muslim 385.

sources.quoted: When the call is heard for the prayer of the day of congregation, haste unto remembrance of Allah

notes: Week-end day (1072–1078): the review looks back at the week's topics.

Hadith numbers to confirm: Abu Dawud 499 ('Abdullah ibn Zayd, the words of the adhan); Abu Dawud 500 (Abu Mahdhura, 'prayer is better than sleep' at fajr); Muslim 385 ('Umar, repeating after the muezzin and answering the hayya'alas with la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah).

The script deliberately gives no counts for the phrases (Sunni practice repeats them; schools differ, e.g. the opening takbir four times or twice in Maliki practice). Keeper may add the counts with a source.
Hook describes the call as a handful of short phrases; no count given.
Pickthall 62:9 quoted from memory, matching earlier days; confirm.
The Shia additions are referenced only by pointing back to day 1071.
